passage:
Salma,
I owe you an explanation for last Thursday. You saw me cry in the middle of the campaign meeting, over a poster. The truth is, I've been giving everything to the tree-protection drive: three meetings a week, the petition, the night vigils. I love it. I also haven't slept properly in a month, and when you asked about the date change, it felt like the last straw. That's not on you. I've made some changes. No campaign messages after ten. Sunday mornings are for cricket and my mother's parathas. And when I need to raise something hard, like my frustration with how the committee runs, I'll do it on a rested day, not at midnight. I still care as much. I just want to still be here next year.
Divyansh

qa.q: How many meetings a week has Divyansh been going to?
qa.a: Three meetings a week.

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling in the campaign meeting?
qa.a: Divyansh felt overwhelmed and exhausted, so a small question felt like the last straw.

qa.q: What changes is Divyansh making to protect the passion?
qa.a: No campaign messages after ten, Sunday mornings kept free, and hard talks saved for rested days.

qa.q: How might Salma feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Salma would likely feel relieved that the tears weren't about Salma, and glad Divyansh is making changes to stay well.

grounding: Shows a young adult who gives everything to a cause, gets overwhelmed, and builds routines and better timing for hard talks.

passage: I'm Harsha, and I do friendship at full volume. When Ritu's father was ill last year, I was at the hospital every evening, cooking, making calls, carrying her bags. I'd do it again. But by the end of that month I was so drained I slept through my own exam. And when Ritu said, gently, that she needed a quiet day, I took it as rejection and cried for hours. It's all big for me: the love, the hurt, the tiredness. What's helping now is pretty boring. I sleep at the same time every night. I walk every morning. And when I need to have a hard talk, I wait till I've eaten and slept, not the minute I'm upset. The waves still come. I'm just learning to surf them.

qa.q: What did Harsha sleep through?
qa.a: Harsha's own exam.

qa.q: How did Harsha feel when Ritu asked for a quiet day?
qa.a: Harsha felt rejected and hurt, crying for hours, because every feeling runs big.

qa.q: What routines are helping Harsha?
qa.a: Sleeping at the same time, walking every morning and waiting to have hard talks until rested and fed.

qa.q: How might Ritu have felt about Harsha's help during her father's illness?
qa.a: Ritu was probably grateful and cared for, though she also needed some quiet time.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult whose intense friendships bring both devotion and exhaustion, and who learns routines to ride the waves.

passage:
Monday: Arohi stayed up till three helping her roommate Sonali through a break-up, then organised the hostel's flood-relief drive before breakfast, buzzing with purpose.
Wednesday: Exhausted, she snapped at the warden, cried in the stairwell and wanted to have it out with Sonali right then about the borrowed clothes. She stopped herself: "Not now. Not tired."
The next Monday: She had slept properly two nights running and kept her morning run. That evening, calm, she raised the clothes with Sonali. It took five minutes. They laughed. The relief drive was still going, and so was she.

qa.q: What did Arohi organise before breakfast on Monday?
qa.a: The hostel's flood-relief drive.

qa.q: How was Arohi feeling on Wednesday?
qa.a: She was exhausted and overwhelmed, snapping and crying in the stairwell.

qa.q: Which choice helped Arohi most, and why?
qa.a: Waiting to talk to Sonali until she was rested, because the hard talk then took five minutes and ended in laughter.

qa.q: How might Sonali experience the talk about the clothes?
qa.a: Sonali likely found it easy and friendly, since Arohi raised it calmly.

grounding: Shows over days a young adult whose passion leads to overwhelm, and who learns timing and routine to keep going.

passage: In the Andheri playground, Neelam fell off the see-saw and burst into tears. Tushar stared at her, then his own lip wobbled and he began to cry too, loudly, though nothing had hurt him. Then he ran to his bag and came back with his favourite toy car. "Here. Car makes better." Neelam, who didn't like cars, cried harder. Tushar looked confused. His mother knelt beside him. "You wanted to help. Neelam likes dolls, na? Let's ask her what would help." Tushar sniffed and asked. Neelam pointed at her mother's lap.

qa.q: What did Tushar bring Neelam?
qa.a: His favourite toy car.

qa.q: Why did Tushar start crying?
qa.a: He felt sad along with Neelam, catching her feeling even though nothing had hurt him.

qa.q: How did Tushar's mother help him learn?
qa.a: She praised his wish to help and showed him to ask Neelam what she needed.

qa.q: How might Neelam feel when offered a car she doesn't like?
qa.a: Neelam may feel more upset, since the gift doesn't fit what she needs.

grounding: Shows a young child who cries when a friend cries and offers his own favourite toy, still learning that feelings differ.

passage:
"Mama, why is Gurleen crying?" Sudha's own eyes were filling up.
"Your little sister is hungry, beta."
Sudha began to sob. "Now I'm sad too!"
"Oh, you're feeling it with her." Mama rocked the baby. "That's kind. But you're not hungry, are you?"
"No. I had idli."
"So it's Gurleen's feeling, and your heart is being her friend."
Sudha ran off and came back with her teddy. "She can have Bhalu."
"That's lovely. Babies can't hold teddies yet. But you can sing to her."
Sudha sat on the floor and sang, still sniffing. The baby quietened.

qa.q: What is Sudha's teddy called?
qa.a: Bhalu.

qa.q: Why did Sudha start to sob?
qa.a: She felt sad along with her baby sister, catching Gurleen's upset.

qa.q: How did Mama help Sudha understand feelings?
qa.a: She explained the hunger was Gurleen's, praised Sudha's kindness and suggested singing instead of the teddy.

qa.q: How might Mama feel watching Sudha sing?
qa.a: Mama is probably touched and pleased by Sudha's caring heart.

grounding: Illustrates a young child who cries with a crying baby and offers a teddy, learning that feelings belong to each person.

passage: Nursery note, Tuesday. When Yamini cried at drop-off today, Seema came and stood very close to her, and within a minute Seema was crying too, just as hard. Then she fetched her own blanket from her cubby and tucked it round Yamini's shoulders. Yamini pushed it away; she wanted her mother, not a blanket. Seema looked hurt and puzzled. I sat with them both and said, "Seema, you felt sad because Yamini was sad. That's kind. Yamini, what would help you?" Yamini said, "Hold my hand." Seema held it. Next step: a picture book about feelings for circle time.

qa.q: What did Seema fetch from her cubby?
qa.a: Her own blanket.

qa.q: How did Seema feel when Yamini pushed the blanket away?
qa.a: Seema felt hurt and puzzled, not yet understanding that Yamini needed something different.

qa.q: What did the note-writer do that helped both girls?
qa.a: Named Seema's kind feeling and asked Yamini what would help, showing that each child's need is her own.

qa.q: What is it like for Yamini at drop-off?
qa.a: Yamini is sad and missing her mother, wanting a hand to hold rather than a blanket.

grounding: Shows a young child who catches a friend's sadness and offers comfort, learning that the friend's feelings are separate.

passage:
"Payal, why are you crying? It's just a drawing."
"It's not just a drawing, Yash. Ma'am put everyone's on the wall except mine."
"I wouldn't care. Mine's never on the wall."
"Well, I care!" Payal wiped her face.
Yash sat down on the step. He didn't get it. Then he remembered how he'd felt when he wasn't picked for the relay. "Is it like being left out?"
"Yes. Like everyone else counts and I don't."
"Oh." He thought. "What happened to it?"
"I think it fell behind the cupboard."
"Let's go and look. And if it's not there, we can ask Ma'am together."
Payal sniffed. "Okay."

qa.q: Where does Payal think her drawing went?
qa.a: Behind the cupboard.

qa.q: How did Yash come to understand Payal's upset?
qa.a: He remembered feeling left out when he wasn't picked for the relay, and saw she felt the same way.

qa.q: What did Yash do that showed growing empathy?
qa.a: He asked what happened and offered to look for the drawing and ask Ma'am together.

qa.q: How did Payal feel about her drawing not being on the wall?
qa.a: Payal felt left out and hurt, as if she didn't count.

grounding: Shows a child beginning to understand a friend's upset he wouldn't share, asking what happened and offering help.

passage: Last term my friend Aditi cried all through lunch because her Nani had moved back to the village. I didn't understand at first. My Dadi lives with us, and sometimes I'd like a bit less of her! But then I remembered how my mother always asks me, "What happened?" before saying anything else. So I asked Aditi. She told me her Nani used to plait her hair every morning and now nobody did. I'm Santosh, and I'm terrible at plaits. But the next day I brought her a hair clip shaped like a mango, and said she could call her Nani from our phone after school. She did. She laughed on the phone. I didn't feel what she felt, exactly. But I got it.

qa.q: What shape was the hair clip?
qa.a: A mango.

qa.q: How did Santosh feel at first about Aditi's crying?
qa.a: Santosh felt puzzled, not understanding why she was so sad, since Dadi at home could be a bit much.

qa.q: What helped Santosh understand and help Aditi?
qa.a: Copying the mother's habit of asking "What happened?" first, then offering a clip and a phone call to Nani.

qa.q: How did Aditi feel after the call with her Nani?
qa.a: Aditi felt happier, laughing on the phone.

grounding: Shows a child learning to understand a friend's sadness they wouldn't feel themselves, by asking what happened as an adult modelled.

passage: Class 4 note, Friday. Something small but lovely today. Bidisha was upset because her team lost the quiz, and Zainab, who doesn't care much about winning, first said, "It's only a quiz." Then she paused. On Monday I had asked the class to try "What happened?" before "It's only". Zainab asked, "Why does it matter so much to you?" Bidisha said her older brother had teased her all week that she'd lose. Zainab nodded slowly. "So it's not the quiz. It's your brother." She sat with Bidisha for the rest of break and helped her write down the answers she'd known. Next step: I will share this, without names, at Monday's circle time.

qa.q: Who had teased Bidisha all week?
qa.a: Her older brother.

qa.q: What did Zainab realise about Bidisha's upset?
qa.a: Zainab understood that Bidisha felt hurt by her brother's teasing, not just sad about losing.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that helped Zainab grow?
qa.a: Taught the class to ask "What happened?" first, and planned to share the example at circle time.

qa.q: How might Bidisha feel when Zainab sits with her?
qa.a: Bidisha probably feels understood and comforted.

grounding: Shows a child moving past her own view to understand why a friend is upset, supported by a teacher who modelled it.

passage:

passage: When Raju's family lost their whole cotton crop to the hailstorm, the news went round the village school in Yavatmal by morning. Avni cried at the back of the class, and at lunch she couldn't eat; she kept saying, "Poor Raju, poor Raju," but when Raju walked past, she looked away, not knowing what to say. Vandana, her cousin, felt oddly calm. She understood exactly what the loss meant: fees, loans, his sister's wedding. She went straight up to Raju, asked what he needed, and wrote out the notes he'd miss while helping in the fields. Only later, walking home, did Vandana wonder why her chest felt so quiet, and Avni's so full.

qa.q: What destroyed Raju's family's crop?
qa.a: The hailstorm.

qa.q: How did Vandana feel on the walk home?
qa.a: She felt puzzled and a little uneasy, wondering why her chest felt so quiet while Avni's felt so full.

qa.q: How did Vandana's kind of empathy help Raju?
qa.a: Her clear understanding led her to ask what he needed and write out the notes he would miss.

qa.q: How might Raju feel when Avni looks away?
qa.a: Raju may feel alone or awkward, not knowing that Avni is actually deeply upset for him.

grounding: Illustrates a teen who understands a friend's loss clearly but feels detached, beside a cousin who feels deeply but freezes.

passage: When Mina's old dog Bruno died, Vera heard at the bus stop in Prague and burst into tears before Mina did. She hugged Mina so hard their glasses clashed, and cried the whole ride to school, until Mina ended up comforting her. At lunch their classmate Tomas, who usually seemed cool and far away, asked Mina calmly, "Do you want to talk about him or not talk about him?" Mina said, "Not talk." Tomas nodded and changed the subject to football, and Mina looked relieved. Vera watched, confused. She had felt everything and helped with nothing. Tomas had felt little, she guessed, and helped exactly. That evening Vera wrote in her notebook: "Next time, ask first."

qa.q: What was the dog's name?
qa.a: Bruno.

qa.q: How did Vera feel watching Tomas help Mina?
qa.a: Vera felt confused and a little ashamed, having felt everything but helped with nothing.

qa.q: What did Vera learn to try next time?
qa.a: To ask the person what they need first, the way Tomas did.

qa.q: How might Mina have felt when she ended up comforting Vera?
qa.a: Mina may have felt tired and a bit burdened, needing comfort herself.

grounding: Shows a teen who feels a friend's pain intensely but helps poorly, learning from a classmate who understands calmly.

passage: Nazia volunteered at the college peer-support desk on Mondays, but lately it felt like every day. Mohit messaged at midnight about his break-up; her roommate cried about marks; two juniors knocked on her door after dinner. She said yes to everyone. By the end of term she was sleeping through lectures and snapping at her own mother on the phone, then feeling guilty. When Mohit texted again at 1 a.m., she felt a flash of resentment that frightened her. At the next volunteer meeting, the counsellor who ran the desk said, "You can care without carrying. You don't have to solve everyone." Nazia put her phone on silent after eleven and started giving people the counsellor's hours instead of her own.

qa.q: When does Nazia volunteer at the desk?
qa.a: On Mondays.

qa.q: What did Nazia feel when Mohit texted at 1 a.m.?
qa.a: She felt a flash of resentment that frightened her, after weeks of exhaustion.

qa.q: What changes helped make Nazia's caring sustainable?
qa.a: Silencing her phone after eleven and pointing people to the counsellor's hours instead of her own.

qa.q: How might Mohit feel if Nazia doesn't reply at 1 a.m.?
qa.a: Mohit may feel a bit let down at first, but he can still reach the counsellor and Nazia the next day.

grounding: Shows a caring young adult who absorbs everyone's problems, grows exhausted and resentful, and learns to care with limits.

passage:
Pooja,
I want to say something carefully, because I care about you. For three months I've been your first call for everything: the fights at home, the exam panic, the flatmate drama. I've loved being there. But I've noticed I'm exhausted, and last week, when you called at 2 a.m., I felt resentful for the first time, and I hated that feeling. I think I've been trying to fix everything instead of just listening. So here's what I can do: I'll always listen when I can, I'll check on you every Sunday, and I'll help you find the college counsellor for the heavy stuff. What I can't do is be awake at 2 a.m. and still be a good friend. I hope that makes sense.
Divyansh

qa.q: When will Divyansh check on Pooja?
qa.a: Every Sunday.

qa.q: How did Divyansh feel after the 2 a.m. call?
qa.a: Divyansh felt resentful for the first time, and hated feeling that way.

qa.q: What limits does Divyansh set, and why are they caring?
qa.a: Listening when possible, a Sunday check-in and help finding the counsellor, so the friendship can last without burning out.

qa.q: How might Pooja feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Pooja may feel a little hurt at first, but also cared for, since the letter is gentle and offers real support.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult exhausted by rescuing a friend, choosing to care with limits and point to professional help.

passage: Everyone calls me the hostel's listening ear. I'm Vijay, twenty-one, and for two years I said yes to every sad person who knocked: Dolma's family problems, my roommate's heartbreak, a junior who was homesick. I'd stay up till four. I thought that's what caring meant. Then one night, when Dolma called crying, I heard myself think, not again, and I felt like a terrible person. My sister said, "You're not a bad friend. You're an empty one." That hit. Now I say, "I can talk for twenty minutes," and I mean it. I point people to the counsellor when it's big. I sleep. And weirdly, I'm kinder now, because I'm not secretly angry.

qa.q: How long does Vijay now offer to talk?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: How did Vijay feel after thinking "not again"?
qa.a: Vijay felt like a terrible person, guilty for the resentment.

qa.q: What changed that made Vijay's caring healthier?
qa.a: Setting a time limit, pointing people to the counsellor for big things and getting sleep.

qa.q: How might Dolma experience the new twenty-minute limit?
qa.a: Dolma may notice Vijay is warmer and more present, even if the calls are shorter.

grounding: Shows a young adult worn out and secretly resentful from absorbing others' problems, who learns to care with limits.

passage: Parveen, you asked how to say no to someone you love. When I was twenty-four, my younger brother Arif kept asking me for money. First for a phone, then a trip, then to pay back a friend. Each time he cried, and I felt every tear as if it were mine. I gave, and gave. One night he asked again, and I, Nazia, did something new. I held his hand and said, "I can see how scared you are. I'm not giving you money this time. But I'll sit with you while you call Abbu and tell him the truth." He shouted at me. Then he called. It was the best thing I ever did for him. Understanding someone, beta, doesn't mean doing everything they ask.

qa.q: What was the third thing Arif wanted money for?
qa.a: To pay back a friend.

qa.q: How did young Nazia feel each time Arif cried?
qa.a: Nazia felt every tear as if it were Nazia's own, pulled to give because of Arif's distress.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: Nazia named Arif's fear but refused the money, offering to sit with him while he called Abbu.

qa.q: How did Arif react to the refusal?
qa.a: He shouted at first, then called Abbu and told the truth.

grounding: Shows an adult who understands a sibling's fear yet refuses to rescue, pairing empathy with a firm boundary.

passage: It was ten at night, the quarterly report was due at nine the next morning, and Noor was on Manjula's doorstep, crying. "Please, can you finish my section too? My mother's been shouting all week, I can't think." Manjula felt the pull at once; she could see how frazzled Noor was, how her hands shook. The old Manjula would have said yes and worked till dawn. She made tea instead. "That sounds really hard, Noor. I'm so sorry about home." She listened for twenty minutes. Then: "I can't write your section. I'll sit with you for an hour while you start it, and I'll help you ask the manager for a day's extension." Noor looked stung. Then she nodded and opened her laptop.

qa.q: When was the quarterly report due?
qa.a: At nine the next morning.

qa.q: What did Manjula feel when she saw Noor crying?
qa.a: She felt a strong pull of sympathy and the old urge to rescue by saying yes.

qa.q: How did Manjula combine empathy with a boundary?
qa.a: She listened and acknowledged Noor's pain, refused to write the section, and offered an hour of company and help asking for an extension.

qa.q: How did Noor react to the boundary?
qa.a: Noor looked stung, then nodded and started working.

grounding: Illustrates an adult who understands a friend's distress without giving in, holding a firm, kind boundary under time pressure.

passage: Rekha's younger brother Hrithik turned up at her Bandra flat with red eyes and a request. He had failed two papers and wanted her to tell their parents he was staying with her "to study", so he could skip going home for Diwali. "You get it, Didi. Papa will explode." She did get it. She remembered her own first failed exam, the dread of the phone call. "I understand why you're scared," she said, sitting beside him. "And I'm not going to lie to them for you." His face fell. "But I'll come with you on Friday and be in the room when you tell them. And afterwards we'll make a study plan together." Hrithik stared at the floor. Then he said, very quietly, "Okay."

qa.q: How many papers had Hrithik failed?
qa.a: Two papers.

qa.q: How was Hrithik feeling when he came to Rekha?
qa.a: He was scared and upset, red-eyed and dreading his father's reaction.

qa.q: What makes Rekha's response both empathetic and firm?
qa.a: She named his fear and remembered her own, but refused to lie and offered to be there when he told them.

qa.q: How might their parents react on Friday, with Rekha in the room?
qa.a: They may still be upset, but calmer, seeing the two of them face it honestly together.

grounding: Shows a young adult understanding a sibling's fear without agreeing to lie, pairing empathy with a firm boundary.

passage:
Monday: At school in Madurai, Naveen argued fiercely in the class debate on whether homework should be banned, waving his hands and making everyone laugh. His teacher, Vasudha-ma'am, praised his sharp points.
Wednesday: At home, when his uncles discussed which college his cousin should choose, Naveen had an opinion, but he kept his eyes down and served the water. In their house, children listened when elders spoke.
The next Sunday: His grandfather asked him directly, "Naveen, what do you think?" Naveen hesitated, glanced at his father, then spoke softly and carefully, his debate voice tucked away but his point just as clear. His grandfather nodded, impressed.

qa.q: What was the class debate about?
qa.a: Whether homework should be banned.

qa.q: How did Naveen feel when his uncles discussed the college choice?
qa.a: He felt he had something to say but held back respectfully, keeping his eyes down.

qa.q: How did Naveen show his personality at home in a way that fit his family?
qa.a: When asked directly, he spoke softly and carefully, keeping his point clear while showing respect.

qa.q: How did Naveen's grandfather react?
qa.a: He nodded, impressed by Naveen's clear, respectful answer.

grounding: Shows a child who voices opinions freely at school but holds back with elders at home, showing personality differently in each place.

passage: Baljeet, you think I was always this talkative? At nine, in our Thrissur house, I didn't say a word at the dinner table. My grandfather sat at the head, and children spoke only when spoken to. I'd look down at my rice even when I thought my uncle was completely wrong about the cricket. But out in the paddy fields with my cousins, I was the boss of every game, making rules, arguing, shouting. My mother noticed. One evening she whispered, "You have a lot to say, don't you?" I, Gopika, nodded. She said, "Say one thing tomorrow. Respectfully." So I told my grandfather, softly, that I liked his old stories. He smiled, for the first time I could remember.

qa.q: Where was young Gopika the boss of every game?
qa.a: Out in the paddy fields with the cousins.

qa.q: How did young Gopika feel at the dinner table?
qa.a: Gopika felt full of opinions but held them back out of respect for the elders.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: The mother's suggestion to say one thing respectfully, which led Gopika to speak to the grandfather.

qa.q: How did the grandfather react when Gopika spoke?
qa.a: He smiled, for the first time Gopika could remember.

grounding: Shows a child who is quiet and modest with elders at home but bold with cousins, and finds a respectful way to speak.

passage: At her aunt's wedding in Jaipur, with two hundred guests and the photographer shouting for poses, Chandrika moved between two worlds all day. With her cousin Madhav and the other children behind the stage, she was loud and bossy, deciding the dance steps and telling everyone exactly what she thought of the DJ's songs. But when her Dadi called her to greet the elders, she lowered her eyes and said only "Namaste," though one great-aunt was saying girls shouldn't dance at all, and Chandrika badly wanted to argue. At the sangeet that night the children performed her dance. The great-aunt clapped loudest. Madhav nudged her: "You should have told her it was yours." Chandrika grinned. "She'll find out."

qa.q: How many guests were at the wedding?
qa.a: Two hundred guests.

qa.q: How did Chandrika feel when the great-aunt said girls shouldn't dance?
qa.a: She felt a strong urge to argue but held back out of respect for the elders.

qa.q: How did Chandrika express herself within her family's expectations?
qa.a: She stayed modest with elders but led the children's dance, letting her work speak for her.

qa.q: How did Madhav see Chandrika's silence?
qa.a: Madhav thought she should have told the great-aunt that the dance was hers.

grounding: Illustrates a child who is bold with cousins but modest with elders, showing her personality differently in each setting.

passage: People think I'm shy. I'm Ishita, fifteen, and I'm not shy. I just learned early that girls in my family don't say, "I want to be a pilot." My aunts would laugh; my grandmother would say, "Be quiet, sit nicely." So I kept the aviation magazines under my mattress and said I wanted to be a teacher, which made everyone nod. Then last month my father, Ramesh, found one of the magazines. I was sure he'd be angry. Instead he sat on my bed and read it with me. He said, "Your grandmother had dreams too, you know. Nobody asked her." Then he said, "Say it out loud, Ishita. Here, where it's safe." So I did. "I want to be a pilot." It felt like breathing.

qa.q: Where did Ishita keep the aviation magazines?
qa.a: Under the mattress.

qa.q: How did Ishita feel when her father found the magazine?
qa.a: She was sure he would be angry and felt scared, then relieved and free when he read it with her.

qa.q: What did Ramesh do that widened what felt safe for Ishita?
qa.a: He read the magazine with her, spoke of her grandmother's unasked dreams and invited her to say her wish aloud.

qa.q: How might Ishita's grandmother have felt as a girl?
qa.a: She may have felt silenced, with dreams nobody ever asked about.

grounding: Shows a teenage girl hiding ambition because of gender rules, and a father who makes it safe to voice it.

passage:
Monday: When Pema's dog died, he wanted to cry, but his uncle said, "Boys don't cry, Pema. Be strong for your mother." So he kept his face still at school and in the courtyard.
Wednesday: He snapped at his friends and couldn't sleep. His mother, Minakshi, found him sitting alone by the empty kennel.
Friday: Minakshi sat beside him. "In this house anyone can cry. Your Papa cried when his father died. I saw." Pema's chin shook, and then the tears came, a long time's worth. Minakshi held him. Afterwards he said, "I miss him so much." "I know," she said. "Me too."

qa.q: Where did Minakshi find Pema?
qa.a: Sitting alone by the empty kennel.

qa.q: How was Pema feeling on Wednesday?
qa.a: He was sad and tense from holding in his grief, snapping at friends and unable to sleep.

qa.q: What did Minakshi do that widened what Pema could show?

passage: You asked why I started the dance club at our school, beta. Years ago I taught a boy called Joseph, fifteen, in Kochi. He danced beautifully, but only when he thought nobody was watching, behind the science block. When I asked him to join the annual day dance, he went red. "My father says dancing is for girls. I'm supposed to play football." So he played football, badly, looking miserable. I, Gargi, went to see his father. I didn't argue; I just showed him a video of Joseph dancing behind the science block. His father watched it twice. Then he said, quietly, "He looks happy." Joseph danced on annual day. His father sat in the front row.

qa.q: Where did Joseph dance when nobody was watching?
qa.a: Behind the science block.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel when asked to join the annual day dance?

grounding: Shows a teenage boy hiding a love of dance because of gender rules, and an adult who helps widen what feels allowed.

passage: I'm Vikas, twenty-two, the eldest of four, and I don't remember a time I wasn't in charge. When Papa's shop closed, I was sixteen. I started tutoring kids after school so my brothers' fees got paid. I learned to fix the pump, fill in forms, talk to the bank. Everyone says, "Vikas is so responsible, just like his father." My father, Ramesh, pats my back. And I am proud of it. But last month a friend asked me what I want to do, just me, and I couldn't answer. I stood in the shower for ages that night, so tired I couldn't think. I think somewhere I stopped wanting things. I'd like to find out what they were.

qa.q: How old was Vikas when Papa's shop closed?
qa.a: Sixteen.

qa.q: How did Vikas feel when asked about wanting something just for Vikas?
qa.a: Vikas felt lost and very tired, unable to answer because those wants had faded.

qa.q: What could Vikas try next to reconnect with those wishes?

grounding: Shows an eldest child whose caring duty became identity, hiding tiredness and forgotten wishes.

passage:

passage: Dolma, you're the eldest too, so listen. At twenty I ran our house in Shillong. My mother was ill, my father worked in the tea gardens, and I had three younger ones to feed, dress and scold. I stopped my college classes for a year. Everybody called me "the second mother". I, Vidya, was proud of that name. But at night I'd sit on the back steps, too tired to cry, and think about the teachers' training course I'd never applied for. One day my aunt came to stay for a month and said, "Go and fill the form. I'll manage." I did. I didn't stop being the eldest. But I found out there was still a me under all that duty.

qa.q: What did everybody call young Vidya?
qa.a: "The second mother."

qa.q: How did young Vidya feel on the back steps at night?
qa.a: Vidya felt too tired to cry and quietly longed for the training course never applied for.

qa.q: How might the aunt have seen Vidya's life?
qa.a: The aunt likely saw a young woman carrying too much and wanted to give her a chance.

grounding: Shows an eldest daughter whose duty became identity, hiding exhaustion and a wish of her own.

passage: At the engineering college hostel in Pune, Varun was known as the loud one: quick jokes in English, first to argue with professors. Nobody there had heard him speak Bundeli, or seen him touch his grandfather's feet. When he went home to the village near Jhansi for Holi, he became quiet and respectful, answering elders in soft Bundeli, letting his uncles decide everything. Back in the hostel, his classmate Parul overheard him on the phone with his grandmother and laughed. "Who is this Varun?" He felt a flash of shame, as if he'd been caught. Then he thought about it. Both voices said what he meant. Both were kind. "Same Varun," he said, grinning. "Two languages."

qa.q: What language does Varun speak with elders at home?
qa.a: Soft Bundeli.

qa.q: How did Varun feel when Parul laughed?
qa.a: He felt a flash of shame, as if caught being someone else.

qa.q: What did Varun realise that turned the moment around?
qa.a: That both voices were honest and kind, so switching was flexibility, not falseness.

qa.q: How might Parul see Varun after his reply?
qa.a: Parul probably sees a new side of him and respects his easy answer.

grounding: Shows a young adult shifting style and language between village and city, and seeing flexibility as a strength.

passage:
Swati,
It's strange. Here in Toronto I call my professors by their first names and argue with them in seminars. I wear shorts to the grocery store. At home in Coimbatore I'd never have spoken to a teacher like that. Then I video-call Amma, and suddenly I'm asking if she's eaten, in Tamil, in my softest voice, and I feel like two different people wearing one face. Some days the switching is tiring. But last week a classmate asked me how I manage both so easily, and I realised: I'm honest in both places. I'm just speaking each place's language. I think that's a skill, not a lie. Tell Appa I'm eating properly.
Naveen

passage: In my village near Ranchi, I'm Trisha-didi: the one who carries water, respects every elder and speaks Kurukh with my grandmother. In Delhi, where I study now, I'm Trisha from the college drama club, loud, in jeans, arguing about plays at midnight. For my first year I felt like a fake in both places. When I went home, my cousin Kamal teased me: "City girl!" When I came back, my friends laughed at my accent. I cried about it once, on the train. Then my drama teacher said something that stuck: "An actor isn't lying when she changes her voice. She's using more of herself." Now I think of it that way. Different rooms, same Trisha.

qa.q: What language does Trisha speak with her grandmother?

qa.q: How did Trisha feel during the first year?

grounding: Shows a young adult moving between village and city who comes to see shifting styles as one honest self.
